stem: Write all the unit vectors in XY-plane.
solution:
Let \(\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j}\) be a unit vector in XY-plane (Fig 10.28). Then, from the figure, we have \(x = \cos\theta\) and \(y = \sin\theta\) (since \(|\vec{r}| = 1\)). So, we may write the vector \(\vec{r}\) as

\(\vec{r}\,(= \overrightarrow{\mathrm{OP}}) = \cos\theta\,\hat{i} + \sin\theta\,\hat{j}\)  ... (1)

Clearly, \(|\vec{r}| = \sqrt{\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta} = 1\)

Also, as \(\theta\) varies from \(0\) to \(2\pi\), the point P (Fig 10.28) traces the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 1\) counterclockwise, and this covers all possible directions. So, (1) gives every unit vector in the XY-plane.

stem: If \(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\), \(2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j}\), \(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}\) and \(\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} - \hat{k}\) are the position vectors of points A, B, C and D respectively, then find the angle between \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}\) and \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CD}}\). Deduce that \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}\) and \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CD}}\) are collinear.
solution:
Note that if \(\theta\) is the angle between AB and CD, then \(\theta\) is also the angle between \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}\) and \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CD}}\).

Now \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}\) = Position vector of B \(-\) Position vector of A

\(= (2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j}) - (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = \hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - \hat{k}\)

Therefore \(|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}| = \sqrt{(1)^{2} + (4)^{2} + (-1)^{2}} = 3\sqrt{2}\)

Similarly \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CD}} = -2\hat{i} - 8\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\) and \(|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CD}}| = 6\sqrt{2}\)

Thus \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}\cdot\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CD}}}{|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}||\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CD}}|} = \dfrac{1(-2) + 4(-8) + (-1)(2)}{(3\sqrt{2})(6\sqrt{2})} = \dfrac{-36}{36} = -1\)

Since \(0 \le \theta \le \pi\), it follows that \(\theta = \pi\). This shows that \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}\) and \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CD}}\) are collinear.

Alternatively, \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CD}}\) which implies that \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}\) and \(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CD}}\) are collinear vectors.

stem: Let \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}\) and \(\vec{c}\) be three vectors such that \(|\vec{a}| = 3\), \(|\vec{b}| = 4\), \(|\vec{c}| = 5\) and each one of them being perpendicular to the sum of the other two, find \(|\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}|\).

Three vectors \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}\) and \(\vec{c}\) satisfy the condition \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = \vec{0}\). Evaluate the quantity \(\mu = \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} + \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}\), if \(|\vec{a}| = 3\), \(|\vec{b}| = 4\) and \(|\vec{c}| = 2\).
solution:
Since \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = \vec{0}\), we have

\(\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}) = 0\)

or \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a} + \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c} = 0\)

Therefore \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c} = -|\vec{a}|^{2} = -9\)  ... (1)

Again, \(\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}) = 0\)

or \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} = -|\vec{b}|^{2} = -16\)  ... (2)

Similarly \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} = -4\)  ... (3)

Adding (1), (2) and (3), we have

\(2(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} + \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}) = -29\)

or \(2\mu = -29\), i.e., \(\mu = \dfrac{-29}{2}\)
_note: BOOK MISPRINT in the printed solution's first step: the book prints the line as \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = \vec{0} = 0\), which is meaningless as an equation and does not yield the next line. The step that actually produces \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a} + \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c} = 0\) is dotting the given condition with \(\vec{a}\), i.e. \(\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}) = 0\) — exactly the form the book itself prints two lines later for \(\vec{b}\). Transcribed here in the self-consistent form; the printed line is verified defective on the page image (p33). The final answer \(\mu = -29/2\) is unaffected.

stem: If with reference to the right handed system of mutually perpendicular unit vectors \(\hat{i}, \hat{j}\) and \(\hat{k}\), \(\vec{\alpha} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{j}\), \(\vec{\beta} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 3\hat{k}\), then express \(\vec{\beta}\) in the form \(\vec{\beta} = \vec{\beta_{1}} + \vec{\beta_{2}}\), where \(\vec{\beta_{1}}\) is parallel to \(\vec{\alpha}\) and \(\vec{\beta_{2}}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{\alpha}\).
solution:
Let \(\vec{\beta_{1}} = \lambda\vec{\alpha}\), \(\lambda\) is a scalar, i.e., \(\vec{\beta_{1}} = 3\lambda\hat{i} - \lambda\hat{j}\).

Now \(\vec{\beta_{2}} = \vec{\beta} - \vec{\beta_{1}} = (2 - 3\lambda)\hat{i} + (1 + \lambda)\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}\).

Now, since \(\vec{\beta_{2}}\) is to be perpendicular to \(\vec{\alpha}\), we should have \(\vec{\alpha}\cdot\vec{\beta_{2}} = 0\). i.e.,

\(3(2 - 3\lambda) - (1 + \lambda) = 0\)

or \(\lambda = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

Therefore \(\vec{\beta_{1}} = \dfrac{3}{2}\hat{i} - \dfrac{1}{2}\hat{j}\) and \(\vec{\beta_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\hat{i} + \dfrac{3}{2}\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}\)

_note: BOOK DEFECT — the stem is transcribed exactly as printed and is UNANSWERABLE as it stands. The clause \(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{d} = 15\) is a scalar equation, not a vector, so "the vector \(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{d} = 15\)" is meaningless; \(\vec{d}\) is never defined in this question. The clause is verbatim the closing condition of Misc Q12 on the same page — a copy-paste corruption. The intended question (the standard NCERT text) is: "show that the vector \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}\) is equally inclined to \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}\) and \(\vec{c}\)", which is consistent with the given hypothesis and with the answer. Verified at 2.6x zoom on the page image (p34) — this is what is printed, not a rendering artefact. Needs an errata bracket at solution-authoring time.
